title: The Hook
text: Before this video goes any further, I want you to try something. Think of the person who knows you best. Can you picture their face? Not just remember what they look like—can you actually see a face in your mind? Now try something different. Silently say, “I need to remember this tomorrow.” Did those words sound like a voice inside your head? Or did you understand the sentence without hearing anything? There are no right answers. And these little tests cannot diagnose anything. But they point to something strange: two people can live in the same world and have very different experiences inside their own minds. Some people see vivid pictures. Some see none. Some experience an almost constant stream of inner words. Others report very little. If you’ve always assumed everybody thinks like you, some of the answers in this video may sound almost impossible. The strange thing is, people on both sides often feel that way. And here’s the question: if our minds can feel so different, how do we know what thinking actually is?

title: The Man Who Lost His Mind’s Eye
text: In 2010, doctors described a man they called MX. He was sixty-five, and something unusual had happened after a heart procedure. Before the procedure, he could picture things in his mind. Afterwards, he couldn’t. He could still recognize objects and remember facts about them, but when he tried to summon an image, nothing appeared. Imagine knowing exactly what your kitchen looks like, but being unable to see it when you close your eyes. A report about MX reached the public. Then people began contacting the researchers with a surprising message: “That’s how my mind has always worked.” These people hadn’t lost their mental pictures. As far as they could remember, they’d never had them. Researchers gave this experience a name: aphantasia. That doesn’t mean people with aphantasia see nothing with their eyes closed—most people just see darkness when they close their eyes. The difference is whether they can create a mental picture. And mental pictures don’t have to look like photographs. For many people, they’re faint, fleeting, or difficult to describe. And here is the surprising part. In one early study, most of the people who reported aphantasia could still see images while dreaming. Their difficulty was with creating pictures on purpose. Here is another way to feel the difference. Try counting the windows in your home without looking around. You may mentally walk from room to room and see each window. Or you might simply know how many there are, without picturing a single room. In research, people with aphantasia were able to do tasks like this, but they described using facts, spatial knowledge, or other strategies instead of pictures. So if a person says they cannot see pictures in their head, can science tell whether they’re really experiencing something different?

title: Can Science Measure an Invisible Picture?
text: One experiment offers a fascinating clue. Look at a bright light, and the pupils in your eyes become smaller. That happens automatically. You don’t have to think about it. In a 2022 study, researchers asked people to look at bright and dark shapes. Then they took the shapes away and asked participants to imagine them. For people who reported having mental images, imagining something bright made their pupils shrink a little—almost as though their eyes were reacting to a real image. In the small group who reported aphantasia, researchers didn’t find that same clear response. This doesn’t mean an eye test can tell you exactly what someone thinks. But it suggests that imagining a picture can have effects on the body—and that those effects differ between people. Another study found something intriguing about emotion. When people read frightening stories, those with aphantasia showed less of a particular physical fear response on average. But when they looked at scary photographs, their responses were comparable to other people’s. The finding doesn’t mean they can’t feel fear. It suggests that imagining a scene and actually seeing one can affect us differently. Now let’s turn to something even more familiar: the voice in your head.

title: Where Does the Inner Voice Come From?
text: Maybe you silently rehearse what to say before an important conversation. Maybe you tell yourself, “Don’t forget the keys.” Or maybe your thoughts rarely take the form of words at all. Psychologists call thinking in inner words inner speech. It can be a full sentence, a fragment, or something that barely feels like a voice. It isn’t the same as hearing a sound coming from outside you. Sometimes you know you’re thinking in words even though there’s no distinct sound. And this is important: having no mental pictures and having little inner speech are not the same thing. We’re looking at two different dimensions of experience, not two names for one condition. One influential explanation comes from watching children. A young child solving a puzzle might say out loud, “Not that piece. This one.” Over time, some of that self-talk becomes silent. But that doesn’t mean everybody uses it equally. Think about how you plan a trip, solve a problem, or rehearse a difficult conversation. Do you talk yourself through the steps, see situations unfolding, or simply move from one decision to the next? Different people may recognize different parts of that description.

title: What Happens When Your Inner Voice Is Quiet?
text: In 2024, researchers compared people who said they had a lot of inner speech with people who said they had very little. They gave both groups a series of tasks. One involved looking at pictures and deciding whether the names of the objects rhymed. Try it yourself. Imagine a picture of a sock next to a clock. Do their names rhyme? Now imagine doing many of those decisions, including tricky ones, without speaking. The two groups answered at roughly the same speed. But the group reporting less inner speech made more mistakes on the rhyming task. The researchers also asked people to remember lists of words that sounded alike. Again, the group with less inner speech found that harder. Does that mean those people are worse at thinking? No. On other tasks, the groups performed similarly. And when participants spoke words out loud to help with the memory task, the gap disappeared. The lesson isn’t that one kind of mind is better. It’s that different people may rely on different tools to solve the same problem. And this study doesn’t prove what is happening in everyone’s head. The groups were selected because they reported very different experiences. Researchers then looked for differences in their performance. That’s useful evidence, but it isn’t a population survey, and it can’t tell us how many people never hear an inner voice.

title: Does Anyone Have No Inner Voice at All?
text: But there’s a catch. Saying you rarely hear words in your mind is not the same as proving you never have inner speech. Researchers still debate where to draw that line. Even the people who study this disagree about what “no inner voice” should mean. Which leads to a much more uncomfortable question: Do we actually know what’s happening in our own heads?

title: The Beeper Experiment
text: Imagine you’re going about an ordinary day. Suddenly, a beep sounds. At that exact moment, you have to notice what was happening in your mind just before the beep. Was there a sentence? A picture? A feeling? Or something harder to describe? [[BEEP]] Psychologist Russell Hurlburt has used a method like this. People carry a device that beeps at unpredictable times. They record what they were experiencing immediately before each beep, and later discuss those moments in careful interviews. In one small study, inner speech appeared in only about a quarter of all sampled moments. Some participants reported it frequently. Others reported none in the moments that were sampled. That does not prove those people never experienced inner speech. But it challenges the idea that everyone is silently talking all day. The researchers also found something especially strange: what they call unsymbolized thinking. Imagine suddenly knowing you should call a friend. There’s no sentence in your mind saying it. No picture of a phone. Just the thought itself. If that sounds impossible to you, it may feel completely ordinary to someone else. Here’s why those interviews matter: the researchers weren’t just asking people to summarize how they usually think. They were asking about specific, fleeting moments. That’s a much harder question, and a reminder that our memories of our own thoughts can be incomplete.

title: Does It Change How We Remember?
text: And this difference can matter in everyday life. People with aphantasia sometimes report that they remember facts about their past without mentally reliving the scenes. Think about your last birthday. Perhaps you can almost see the room and the faces. Another person might remember who was there, what everyone said, and why it mattered, without replaying a single image. Both people remember the event, but their experiences of remembering can be very different. Yet studies have also found that they can perform just as accurately as other people on certain visual memory tasks, using different strategies. So a missing mental picture doesn’t mean a missing memory, or a lack of intelligence. And the opposite extreme exists too. Some people describe mental images so vivid they almost resemble real sight. Even among people who can visualize, the experience can vary enormously. What seems obvious or effortless to one person may be completely unfamiliar to another.

title: The Final Question
text: Think back to the beginning. Could you see a face? Did you hear a sentence? Were there words, images, both, or neither? Those moments are clues, not labels. They don’t tell you everything about how your mind works. But they reveal something easy to forget: Your own experience of thinking isn’t the only possible one. A thought can come as a voice, a picture, a feeling—or simply as knowing. And that raises one last question. Someone close to you might have an inner world completely unlike yours. Have you ever asked them what it’s like?
